prompt: """Naive baseline: match an utterance against the hard-coded intent taxonomy. Each intent is represented by the TF-IDF centroid of its taxonomy examples (data/taxonomy.json). An utterance is scored by cosine similarity to every intent centroid; the top intent wins. Anything whose best score is below THRESHOLD is sent to out_of_scope. This is deliberately simple. Swapping TF-IDF for a sentence-embedding model is one obvious next step, but the way this is built has other problems worth finding. """ import json from pathlib import Path import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer from sklearn.preprocessing import normalize DATA = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" THRESHOLD = 0.10          # below this best-match score we call it out_of_scope def load_taxonomy():     tax = json.load(open(DATA / "taxonomy.json", encoding="utf-8"))     return [i["name"] for i in tax["intents"]], {i["name"]: i["examples"] for i in tax["intents"]} def clean(text):     return " ".join(str(text).lower().split()) class TaxonomyMatcher:     def __init__(self):         self.intents, self.examples = load_taxonomy()         train = pd.read_csv(DATA / "train.csv")         dev = pd.read_csv(DATA / "dev.csv")         corpus = [clean(t) for t in pd.concat([train.utterance, dev.utterance])]   # vocabulary / idf source         corpus += [clean(e) for ex in self.examples.values() for e in ex]         self.vec = TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True).fit(corpus)         self.centroids = self._build_centroids()     def _build_centroids(self):         rows = []         for name in self.intents:             ex = self.examples[name]             if not ex:                 rows.append(np.zeros(len(self.vec.vocabulary_)))      # no examples -> never matches                 continue             m = np.asarray(self.vec.transform([clean(e) for e in ex]).mean(axis=0)).ravel()             rows.append(m)         return normalize(np.vstack(rows))     def scores(self, utterances):         X = normalize(self.vec.transform([clean(u) for u in utterances]))         return np.asarray(X @ self.centroids.T)                        # (n, n_intents) cosine     def predict(self, utterances):         s = self.scores(utterances)         pred = [self.intents[i] for i in s.argmax(1)]         best = s.max(1)         return [("out_of_scope" if b < THRESHOLD else p) for p, b in zip(pred, best)], s if __name__ == "__main__":     import argparse     ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Write predictions for data/test.csv in the submission format.")     ap.add_argument("--out", default=str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "submissions" / "baseline_predictions.csv"))     a = ap.parse_args()     test = pd.read_csv(DATA / "test.csv")     pred, _ = TaxonomyMatcher().predict(test.utterance.tolist())     pd.DataFrame({"id": test["id"], "intent": pred}).to_csv(a.out, index=False)     print("wrote", a.out, len(pred)) i want line by line code """Evaluate the baseline on the dev set and write results/baseline_dev.json. Run:  python -m baseline.eval      (from the task-repo folder) Note: dev labels are SILVER (noisy), so numbers here are a guide, not the truth. """ import json from pathlib import Path import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report, confusion_matrix, f1_score from baseline.baseline import DATA, TaxonomyMatcher RESULTS = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "results" def top_k_and_mrr(scores, intents, y_true, k=3):     idx = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(intents)}     ranks = []     for s, y in zip(scores, y_true):         order = np.argsort(-s)         ranks.append(int(np.where(order == idx[y])[0][0]) + 1)     ranks = np.array(ranks)     return float((ranks <= k).mean()), float((1.0 / ranks).mean()) def main():     dev = pd.read_csv(DATA / "dev.csv")     m = TaxonomyMatcher()     pred, scores = m.predict(dev.utterance.tolist())     y = dev.intent.tolist()     top1 = accuracy_score(y, pred)     top3, mrr = top_k_and_mrr(scores, m.intents, y, k=3)     macro_f1 = f1_score(y, pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0)           # reported as macro-F1     report = classification_report(y, pred, target_names=m.intents, output_dict=True, zero_division=0)     cm = confusion_matrix(y, pred).tolist()     out = {         "n_dev": len(dev),         "top1_accuracy": round(top1, 4),         "top3_accuracy": round(top3, 4),         "mrr": round(mrr, 4),         "macro_f1": round(macro_f1, 4),         "per_class": {k: {kk: round(vv, 4) for kk, vv in v.items()} for k, v in report.items() if k in m.intents},         "confusion_matrix": cm,         "note": "dev labels are silver (noisy). See README.",     }     RESULTS.mkdir(exist_ok=True)     json.dump(out, open(RESULTS / "baseline_dev.json", "w"), indent=2)     print(f"dev n={len(dev)}  top1={top1:.3f}  top3={top3:.3f}  MRR={mrr:.3f}  macro-F1={macro_f1:.3f}")     for k in m.intents:         r = out["per_class"][k]         print(f"  {k:18s} P={r['precision']:.2f} R={r['recall']:.2f} F1={r['f1-score']:.2f} n={int(r['support'])}") if __name__ == "__main__":     main() explain each line of the code and what it does and overall

Stage 2: Feature Interaction (Attention Mechanisms) If you move to transformer-based embeddings (like BGE or MiniLM), you are implicitly leveraging attention. Here is how you extract meaning from it: - Choice A: Single [CLS] Token Extraction - How it works: Uses the self-attention mechanism of the transformer to pool all the information of the sentence into the first token ([CLS]). - Pros: Standard, fast, and gives a fixed-size vector for the entire utterance. - Choice B: Mean Pooling (over Multi-Head Self-Attention output) - How it works: Instead of just the [CLS] token, you average the contextualized embeddings of every word in the sentence. - Why choose this: Multi-head attention allows different heads to track different linguistic features (e.g., Head 1 tracks action verbs, Head 2 tracks food items). Mean pooling often yields slightly better sentence-level representations than the [CLS] token. - Choice C: Cross-Attention (Cross-Encoder Architecture) - How it works: Instead of embedding the utterance independently, you feed [Utterance] + [SEP] + [Intent Description] into the transformer simultaneously. The attention heads calculate the correlation between every word in the utterance and every word in the intent description. - Pros: Absolute maximum accuracy. - Cons: Extremely slow. Stage 3: Classification & Similarity (The Decision Engine) Now that you have vectors, how do you decide which intent wins? The baseline used Centroids + Cosine Similarity. Now that you have train.csv, you have better options. - Choice A: Centroid + Cosine Similarity (Zero-Shot) - Mathematics: Averages all vectors of an intent into one point. - Flaw: Suffers from "Centroid Collapse." If users ask for "Order Food" in two distinct ways (e.g., "I'm hungry" vs "Add burger to cart"), the average of these two clusters sits in the empty space between them. - Choice B: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) - Mathematics: Finds the  closest training examples to the test utterance and takes a majority vote. - Pros: Solves the multimodal problem. It doesn't average anything; it just looks for local clusters in the vector space. - Choice C: Parametric Classifier (SVM or Logistic Regression) - How it works: You freeze your embedding model, generate vectors for the 30k training rows, and train an SVM on top. - Pros: Extremely fast to train. SVMs find the optimal hyperplanes between intent clusters, handling overlapping boundaries much better than Cosine Similarity. - Choice D: Fully Supervised Neural Head (End-to-End) - How it works: Add a Linear Layer + Softmax function on top of your transformer. Train the whole thing end-to-end on train.csv using Cross-Entropy Loss. - Pros: The weights of the classifier and the embedding space are co-optimized. Stage 4: Out-of-Scope (OOS) Detection & Confidence Scoring You must reject queries that don't fit the 12 intents. - Choice A: Absolute Distance Thresholding (Cosine/L2) - How it works: If the max similarity score is , reject it. - Flaw: Neural embeddings are notoriously uncalibrated. A dense embedding model might give a 0.60 cosine similarity to complete gibberish just because vectors live in a tight hypersphere. - Choice B: Softmax Thresholding - How it works: If the highest probability from your neural classifier is , reject it. - Flaw: Standard Softmax pushes the highest value toward 1.0, making the model overconfident even on OOS data. - Choice C: Temperature Scaling (Calibration) - Mathematics: You divide the logits by a temperature scalar  (e.g., ) before applying Softmax: . - Pros: Softens the probability distribution. It forces the model to be mathematically honest about its uncertainty, making threshold-based OOS detection drastically more accurate. explain the best choice and why
